bigPicture: Nvidia's co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive after reports of an affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, with finance chief Colette Kress taking over for now; the shares fell as much as about 14% before recovering much of the loss, dragging chipmakers in Asia. Bets on a US interest-rate rise in December pushed the 10-year Treasury yield above 5%, sent the euro to its weakest since April 2025 and cut gold by nearly 3%, while oil rebounded toward $95 after President Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran. In Moscow, Vladimir Putin met US envoys for about two and a half hours without a breakthrough, as leaders of nearly 50 European countries met in Dublin to discuss Ukraine's security. European shares still closed at a record and Warsaw's WIG20 rose 1.7% on its first session after the Independence Day holiday.

glossary.def: A country whose economy and financial markets are developing and opening to foreign investors; there is no single definition, and institutions such as the IMF, the World Bank and MSCI classify countries differently.
glossary.example: MSCI still classifies Poland as an emerging market, while FTSE Russell has counted it as developed since 2018.

glossary.def: The tendency of poorer economies to grow faster than richer ones because extra capital and copied technology add more output when a country starts from a lower level.
glossary.example: Poland's income per person rose from 44% to 81% of the EU average between 1995 and 2025.

glossary.def: The difference between the yields on two bonds, usually quoted in basis points; it shows how much extra return lenders demand for one borrower compared with another.
When a borrower earns income in one currency but owes debts in another, so a fall in its income currency raises the debt burden.
glossary.example: A Polish firm with złoty revenue and a dollar loan owes more in złoty when USD/PLN rises.

glossary.def: An abrupt halt in foreign lending and investment into a country, forcing it to cut spending or let its currency fall sharply.
glossary.example: During the 1997 Asian crisis, foreign banks stopped renewing loans to firms in Thailand and Indonesia.

glossary.def: Push factors are conditions in rich countries (such as US interest rates) that send money abroad or bring it home; pull factors are conditions in the receiving country (growth, stability) that attract it.
glossary.example: Higher expected Fed rates are a push factor drawing money out of emerging markets.

glossary.def: A temporary chief executive who runs a company until a permanent one is appointed.
glossary.example: Nvidia's finance chief Colette Kress became interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigned.

glossary.def: Government rules that restrict selling certain goods or technology abroad, usually for national-security reasons.
glossary.example: The US limits sales of its most advanced AI chips to China.

glossary.def: Tankers with opaque ownership and insurance used to move oil while avoiding sanctions or price caps.
glossary.example: UK sanctions target shipping networks that carry Russian oil.

glossary.def: A range around a central bank's inflation target within which inflation is considered acceptable.
glossary.example: India targets 4% inflation with a 2–6% band; October's 6.09% was above it.

glossary.def: A situation in which people's lack of food threatens their lives or livelihoods, often meaning skipped meals or selling assets to eat.
glossary.example: UN agencies say over one million people in Lebanon face acute food insecurity.

glossary.def: The time between catching an infection and showing symptoms.
glossary.example: Ebola's maximum incubation period is 21 days, so outbreaks are declared over after 42 days with no new cases.

glossary.def: A scheduled update of which companies are in an index and in what weights, which forces funds that track the index to buy or sell.
glossary.example: Strategy will leave MSCI's indices at the close of 30 November.

glossary.def: A business that sells fake or low-quality research papers or authorship to academics.
glossary.example: IEEE retracted 1,400 conference papers linked to paper mills in one day.

glossary.def: Replacing direct use of fuels (petrol, gas, coal) with electricity in transport, heating and industry.
glossary.example: A COP31 pledge aims for electricity to supply 35% of final energy use by 2035.

In Europe, Burberry jumped about 8% after returning to profit and Munich Re and Allianz rose after strong results, helping the Stoxx 600 to a record. stories.everyday: Many pension funds and index funds, including those held by Polish savers through global ETFs, own Nvidia because it is one of the biggest companies in the S&P 500; a sharp swing in one stock can visibly move their value. The story is also a reminder that the AI chips behind chatbots and data centres are now treated as a national-security matter.
stories.rankWhy: Nvidia is one of the world's most valuable companies and the bellwether of the AI boom, so its leader's sudden exit hit chip stocks from Taipei to New York and raised US–China security questions.
stories.title: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO; finance chief Colette Kress takes over for now and chip stocks swing
stories.what: Nvidia said on Thursday that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member 'effective immediately', after 33 years at the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress becomes interim CEO while keeping her finance job, and former Synopsys boss Harvey C. Jones becomes the board's first-ever chair; the board will look at internal and external candidates for a permanent CEO. AP and Al Jazeera report the resignation followed reports of an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at Singapore-based Nvidia partner Megaspeed whom US officials reportedly concluded was a Chinese spy, and of a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reported to him; China denied trying to ensnare him and Nvidia said it had 'no reason to believe' national security or its secrets were compromised. Nvidia shares fell as much as about 14% after the opening bell (day's low $148.80 vs Wednesday's $173.73 close) before recovering to roughly 4–5% lower by early afternoon in New York, according to Motley Fool and Yahoo Finance data. Results for the quarter are still due on Tuesday 17 November, the company said.
stories.why: Investors pay a premium for companies whose strategy is closely tied to one founder; when that person leaves suddenly, they price in more uncertainty about strategy and customer relationships. The allegations also touch the most sensitive issue in the chip industry, US export controls on advanced AI chips to China, so analysts quoted by AP and Reuters saw possible political and legal risk on top of the leadership gap. Because Nvidia is such a large part of US indices and supplies the whole AI build-out, its fall dragged Asian chipmakers (Taiwan's index fell about 2.6–3%) while rival AMD rose about 5–6% on an analyst upgrade, Motley Fool reported.

stories.everyday: For Poland, any deal shapes the security of its eastern border, defence spending and the future of about a million Ukrainian refugees living in the country. A larger prisoner exchange would bring home soldiers and civilians held for years.
stories.rankWhy: Talks on ending Europe's biggest war since 1945 affect the security of Poland and the whole continent, energy prices and millions of Ukrainians.
stories.title: Putin meets US envoys Witkoff and Kushner for over two hours; Kremlin calls talks 'useful' but no breakthrough as Europe meets in Dublin
stories.what: Russian President Vladimir Putin met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the Kremlin on Thursday for more than two hours (Interfax-Ukraine put it at about two and a half), according to Russian media; Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov called the talks substantive and useful and said both sides agreed to continue three-way talks with Ukraine. Putin called the possible presence of foreign troops in Ukraine a threat to Russia's security and proposed a humanitarian operation in the Donetsk-region town of Kostiantynivka, which the Kremlin said the US side supported; Ukraine disputes that Russia controls the town. The meeting followed US–Ukraine–Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November that agreed in principle on what Kushner called the war's largest prisoner exchange, with a Russian official saying more than 1,000 per side could be swapped within weeks, but no breakthrough on territory or a ceasefire. In Dublin, leaders of nearly 50 countries met at the European Political Community summit, where President Zelensky said Europe must have a place in any negotiations; no decision on a single EU negotiator was reported, the Irish Times said. After the summit, European Council President António Costa said the European Commission will propose within weeks how to cover Ukraine's extra €70 billion financing need, for EU leaders to discuss on 26–27 November, Trend reported.
stories.why: Russia wants a settlement to cover wider 'European security architecture', which European leaders resist because it could touch NATO's presence near Russia's borders, the Irish Times reported. The US is acting as a go-between, so the envoys were due to brief Zelensky after Moscow; Putin and Trump may discuss Ukraine at the APEC summit in China later this month, according to the Kremlin readout reported by UNN and HNGN.

stories.everyday: A stronger dollar makes anything priced in dollars, such as fuel, electronics and imported raw materials, more expensive in złoty terms. For Poles with savings in gold the fall cuts their value; for people planning US holidays or buying from US shops, the dollar near 4 zł makes it costlier.
stories.rankWhy: Higher US interest-rate expectations move borrowing costs, currencies and gold worldwide, including the złoty and Polish loan rates.
stories.title: Fed rate-hike bets push the US 10-year yield above 5%, the euro to its weakest since April 2025 and gold down nearly 3%
stories.what: After hotter-than-expected US October inflation data on Tuesday, traders are pricing an almost certain Federal Reserve rate rise at its December meeting: Reuters cited fed funds futures implying an 87% chance of a 0.25-point rise and a 13% chance of a 0.5-point rise, while Trading Economics cited about 90% odds for a hike; Fed Governor Christopher Waller said this week a half-point move should be considered if core inflation stays hot, and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said at least two more quarter-point rises are needed, Kitco reported. The 10-year US Treasury yield (the interest rate on 10-year government debt) rose to roughly 5.08–5.12% on Thursday, and the dollar index reached its highest since April 2025. The euro fell about 0.3% to around $1.106, its weakest since April 2025, Boursorama reported, and gold dropped about 2.7–3% to around $3,880 an ounce. US weekly jobless claims rose by 9,000 to 200,000, slightly above forecasts, the Labor Department said.
stories.why: When markets expect higher US rates, dollar assets pay more, so money flows into the dollar and out of other currencies. Gold pays no interest, so when bond yields rise, holding gold costs more in missed interest, and a stronger dollar makes gold dearer for buyers using other currencies; analysts quoted by Business Recorder and Trading Economics cited both. Higher US yields also tend to lift borrowing costs elsewhere because global investors compare returns across countries.

stories.everyday: Fuel and heating costs follow oil and gas with a lag of weeks; a renewed rise could slow the recent fall in petrol prices at Polish stations and keeps winter heating bills uncertain. In the US, households heating with oil are expected to pay about 70% more this winter, according to US energy assistance directors cited by AP.
stories.rankWhy: Oil prices feed into fuel, heating and transport costs everywhere, and the Strait of Hormuz remains the world's most important oil chokepoint.
stories.title: Oil rebounds toward $95 after Trump says the US 'doesn't need' a deal with Iran; European gas jumps about 6%
stories.what: Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, rose to roughly $94–95 a barrel on Thursday, up about 1% by late morning according to Oilprice.com and about 2.5–2.7% later in the day according to Trading Economics, with US WTI near $88; it was a second day of gains after a ten-week low of about $91.5 on Tuesday. Oilprice.com reported that President Trump wrote on Truth Social that the US does not need a deal with Iran, saying Washington controls Iran's money and the Strait of Hormuz; Iran's security council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran would not send any enriched nuclear material out of the country. Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed this week that several tankers trying to use routes it had not approved struck mines in the strait; neither side has offered evidence, AP reported. European gas (Dutch TTF) jumped about 6% to around €92 per megawatt-hour on colder weather forecasts, an outage reducing Norwegian supply from the Troll field, and EU storage below 72% versus a five-year average of 89%, Trading Economics reported.
stories.why: Oil had fallen about 25% from its late-October peak of $118 as traders hoped for diplomacy, Oilprice.com said; a statement suggesting no deal is needed revives the risk that shipping through Hormuz stays disrupted. At the same time, Saudi Arabia reported a 26% jump in October output and US crude stocks rose by about 4.7 million barrels, which limits how far prices climb. Gas prices react to weather because heating demand rises quickly in a cold snap, and low storage leaves less buffer.

stories.everyday: Power cuts in winter mean no heating, water pumps or lifts for families; they also push more Ukrainians to seek safety abroad, including in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: Daily attacks on cities and the power grid as Ukraine enters its fifth winter of war affect millions of civilians.
stories.title: Russian attacks kill at least 10 and injure 40 across Ukraine in a day, including at a market in Odesa region, as envoys meet Putin
stories.what: Russian missile and drone attacks killed 10 people and injured 40 across Ukraine over the past day, according to local authorities cited by the Kyiv Independent on Thursday. At least four people were killed and eight injured at a market in Chornomorsk in Odesa region, and one person was killed in Kyiv. Overnight, Russia launched ballistic and Zircon missiles plus 123 long-range attack drones, of which Ukraine said it intercepted 89 drones and 5 Banderol/Dan-T missile-drones by 8 a.m.; more than 160 settlements in Rivne region lost power.
stories.why: Russia has been targeting energy infrastructure and cities as winter starts, while Ukraine is short of Patriot air-defence interceptors, the Irish Times reported. The strikes continued during the diplomacy in Abu Dhabi and Moscow, which has not produced a ceasefire.

stories.everyday: Many European factories, including Polish suppliers to car makers, are part of supply chains that run through Mexico to the US; trade shocks there can reach orders in Europe. For the migrants, mostly fleeing poverty and violence, the dispute decides whether they are turned back.
stories.rankWhy: Mexico is one of the largest US trading partners, so a threat to double tariffs puts supply chains for cars, food and electronics at risk, though no measure has been issued yet.
stories.title: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico unless it stops a migrant caravan; Sheinbaum says no caravan has reached the US border
stories.what: President Trump wrote on social media on Thursday that he would double tariffs on Mexico if it does not stop a group of migrants heading north, saying there would be 'no leniency', the Jerusalem Post (citing wire reports) reported. The group of roughly 1,500 people, mostly Central Americans by one estimate, left the southern Mexican city of Tapachula on Tuesday. President Claudia Sheinbaum replied that no caravan has reached the US border since 2025, that migrants are being returned to their home countries, and that there would be no repression. The peso weakened about 0.2% to roughly 18.63 per dollar, El Financiero reported, citing Bloomberg data.
stories.why: A tariff is a tax on imports paid when goods cross the border, so doubling it would raise costs for US buyers of Mexican goods and hurt Mexican exporters. Mexican outlet UnoTV noted a legal hurdle: in February 2026 the US Supreme Court ruled that the emergency-powers law (IEEPA) cannot be used to impose tariffs, so any increase would need another legal basis such as trade-law sections 232, 301 or 122. The small peso move suggests traders see the threat as a negotiating tactic for now, analysts at Banco Base suggested.

stories.everyday: Sanctions are one of the main tools Europe uses instead of direct military involvement; how well they work affects the length of the war on Poland's border.
stories.rankWhy: Sanctions on oil producers and tankers aim to cut the revenue that pays for Russia's war, with knock-on effects for oil shipping.
stories.title: UK sanctions all ten of Russia's largest oil producers and more shipping networks, and urges allies in Dublin to follow
stories.what: Britain announced a new sanctions package on Thursday aimed at Russia's energy and shipping sectors, saying it is now the only country to have sanctioned all of Russia's top ten oil producers, the Kyiv Independent reported. The government said the package targets Slavneft (the last of the ten not yet listed), Rosneft's Arctic project Vostok Oil, major coal companies, trading networks and 'shadow fleet' tankers carrying Russian oil and LNG. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said pressure on Russia must keep rising to secure a full and immediate ceasefire, and was due to urge other leaders at the Dublin summit to do the same.
stories.why: Oil and gas exports are Russia's biggest source of foreign income; sanctions make it harder and costlier to sell, insure and ship that oil, which can force bigger discounts. Their effect depends on enforcement, because 'shadow fleet' tankers and traders in third countries can keep some trade going.

stories.everyday: In India, food takes a large share of poorer families' spending, so food inflation hits them hardest. India also illustrates a lesson for Poland: inflation can rise even when industry is doing fine if harvests fail.
stories.rankWhy: India is the world's most populous country, and food-led inflation above the central bank's 6% ceiling squeezes hundreds of millions of household budgets.
stories.title: India's inflation jumps to 6.09%, above the central bank's tolerance band, on food prices; a December rate rise looks likely to economists
stories.what: India's consumer price inflation rose to 6.09% in October from 5.54% in September, the highest of 2026, official data released on Thursday showed, ThePrint and ANI reported. Food and beverage prices, about 37% of the price basket, rose 8.51% from a year earlier, led by milk, sugar and onions; rural inflation (6.63%) ran above urban (5.41%). The Reserve Bank of India targets 4% inflation with a tolerance band of 2–6%. ICRA chief economist Aditi Nayar said a 25-basis-point rate rise at the 2–4 December policy meeting appears almost certain.
stories.why: ThePrint reported that a weak monsoon and low reservoir levels threaten the winter crop, pushing up food prices, while a low base from last year (when prices barely rose) lifts the annual rate. When inflation runs above target, central banks raise interest rates to cool spending and borrowing.

stories.everyday: Poland is going through exactly this shift, with heat pumps, electric cars and new wind and solar farms; global deals affect EU climate rules and therefore energy bills in Poland.
stories.rankWhy: The UN climate talks shape the energy policies of nearly 200 countries, but major leaders are absent and divisions over fossil fuels remain deep.
stories.title: COP31 in Antalya: a voluntary pledge to raise electricity's share of energy use to 35% by 2035 splits countries, as Guterres calls for windfall taxes
stories.what: At the UN climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye (9–20 November), a voluntary pact launched this week aims to raise electricity's share of final energy use to 35% by 2035, from an estimated 20–23% today, Energynews.pro reported. Australia joined, and officials from Germany, Ethiopia, Norway and Pakistan expressed support, but India refused to sign and the EU wants the extra electricity to be explicitly clean. UN Secretary-General António Guterres urged countries to end dependence on fossil fuels and to tax oil and gas companies' windfall profits, allAfrica and Al Jazeera reported. Leaders of the US, China, India, France, Germany and Japan are absent.
stories.why: Electrifying transport, heating and industry lets countries use solar and wind power instead of burning oil and gas directly, but it only cuts emissions if the electricity itself is low-carbon, which is why the EU objects to the wording. Saudi Arabia, India and China are expected to resist stronger language on leaving fossil fuels, Energynews.pro reported.

stories.everyday: Rising European share prices lift the value of pension funds and ETFs that many Europeans, including Poles saving in PPK schemes, hold. Burberry's results suggest some recovery in demand for luxury goods after a weak period.
stories.rankWhy: Strong company results kept European shares at records even as the US AI trade wobbled, which matters for European pension and savings funds.
stories.title: European shares close at a record as Burberry, Munich Re and Allianz beat forecasts, while chip stocks fall with Nvidia
stories.what: The Stoxx 600 rose about 0.2–0.25% to a second straight record close of about 664, Boursorama and Investing.com reported. Burberry jumped about 8% after returning to a first-half profit (pre-tax profit of £19 million against a £48 million loss a year earlier), Share Talk reported; Munich Re rose about 3% after better-than-expected third-quarter results, and Allianz about 2% after raising the top of its 2026 operating-profit outlook, according to Trading Economics. Siemens gained after raising its medium-term targets on record train orders and data-centre demand. Semiconductor and software stocks fell in sympathy with Nvidia, and UK gold miner Endeavour Mining fell 8.5% after warning on output at its Mana mine in Burkina Faso.
stories.why: European firms are on track for about 25% quarterly profit growth, the strongest in four years according to LSEG data cited by Reuters, while Europe has less exposure to AI chip stocks than the US or Asia. That has led some investors to rotate money into European banks, insurers and industrials, Reuters reported.

stories.everyday: Allegro is where millions of Poles shop online, and its growth reflects strong consumer spending. Many Polish pension funds (OFE and PPK) own Allegro shares, so its price matters for retirement savings.
stories.rankWhy: Allegro is Poland's biggest online marketplace, used by about 15.8 million Polish buyers, and its rise led the WIG20 to a 1.7% gain.
stories.title: Allegro beats forecasts and raises its 2026 targets; its shares jump 5% and lead the WIG20 up 1.7%
stories.what: Allegro reported third-quarter revenue of 3.41 billion zł (up 20% year on year), adjusted EBITDA of 1.13 billion zł (up 23%) and net profit of 575 million zł (up 45%), all above the PAP Biznes analyst consensus, Strefa Inwestorów reported. It raised its 2026 guidance: group GMV (the value of goods sold on the platform) is now expected to grow 15–16% and adjusted EBITDA 22–24%. It also signed a logistics agreement with parcel-locker operator InPost running to the end of 2031 and worth at least 8 billion zł, ending an arbitration dispute between them, Parkiet and Forex Club reported. The shares rose 5.1%, the biggest gain in the WIG20, which closed up 1.69% at 4,279.50 on the first session after Wednesday's Independence Day holiday; KGHM fell 1.3% as copper prices fell, XYZ.pl reported.
stories.why: Allegro said Polish GMV grew at its fastest pace in four years with record margins, without raising seller commissions, and that its foreign business is still roughly doubling each year. Results that beat expectations make investors raise their estimates of future profits, which supports a higher share price. Warsaw also caught up with gains in Western Europe on Wednesday, when the market was closed.

stories.everyday: Acute food insecurity means families skip meals or sell belongings to eat; WFP said even a small new shock can push them deeper into crisis.
stories.rankWhy: About a quarter of Lebanon's population faces acute hunger after two wars and a six-year economic crisis.
stories.title: More than one million people in Lebanon, nearly a quarter of the population, face acute food shortages, UN agencies say
stories.what: A joint statement from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization, the World Food Programme and Lebanon's agriculture ministry said more than one million people face acute food insecurity, a number expected to rise to 1.15 million by mid-2027, Al Jazeera reported. The war that began in March 2026 displaced over a million people; about 300,000 remain displaced since fighting eased in June.
stories.why: The agencies blamed two conflicts in under two years, a weak economy with few jobs and depleted savings, and rising food and fuel costs. Lebanon has been in economic crisis since 2019 and has not completed the reforms needed for an IMF bailout.

stories.everyday: Refugees in makeshift shelters face shortages of food, clean water and health care; aid groups report rising malnutrition.
stories.rankWhy: Tens of thousands of people are fleeing violence in northern Nigeria into Niger, one of the world's poorest countries.
stories.title: Nearly 64,000 Nigerians have fled to Niger this year to escape militant and gang violence, UNHCR says
stories.what: The UN refugee agency said nearly 64,000 Nigerians have crossed into Niger since January, bringing the total of Nigerians sheltering there to about 327,500, Vanguard reported. Most arrive in Diffa and Tahoua regions; more than two-thirds of the 23,000 arrivals in Diffa are children, and only about 5% of this year's arrivals are formally registered. UNHCR is seeking $11.4 million for Niger, Nigeria and Benin.
stories.why: Islamist militants and armed criminal gangs in northern Nigeria are driving people out, UNHCR said; registration gaps limit access to aid.

stories.everyday: Tracing and monitoring every contact is what stops one imported case from becoming an epidemic.
stories.rankWhy: Kenya containing its imported cases is a rare piece of good news in Congo's huge Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak.
stories.title: Kenya discharges its last Ebola patient and starts a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free
stories.what: Kenya discharged its final Ebola patient, bringing recoveries to seven, and began a 42-day countdown to being declared free of the disease, allAfrica and the WHO Director-General reported. No new confirmed cases have been reported in Kenya since 20 October, and all 135 contacts completed 21 days of monitoring. In Congo, where the outbreak began, the WHO counts almost 11,000 confirmed cases and more than 5,300 deaths.
stories.why: An outbreak is declared over after 42 days, twice the 21-day maximum incubation period, without new cases. Kenya also urged countries with Ebola-related travel restrictions to reconsider them.

stories.everyday: Big listings can pull money from other tech shares as funds make room for the new stock, which can move global index funds held by ordinary savers.
stories.rankWhy: One of the largest stock-market listings ever planned would test investor appetite for AI companies in a nervous week.
stories.title: AI firm Anthropic sets its share sale for 18 November, with trading from 19 November, at a valuation of up to about $1.45 trillion
stories.what: Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, plans to price its initial public offering on Wednesday 18 November and begin trading on Thursday 19 November under the ticker ANT, Yahoo Finance reported on Thursday. It is offering about 825 million shares at $70–78 each, implying a valuation of roughly $1.3–1.45 trillion. The filing shows revenue of $33.2 billion in the first nine months of 2026 and an operating loss of $1.3 billion, Yahoo Finance said.
stories.why: An IPO (initial public offering) is when a private company first sells shares to the public; the price range is set from investor demand gathered during a roadshow. The timing comes as investors reassess AI valuations after Nvidia's leadership shock.

stories.everyday: The same AI tools that help office workers can also help attackers, which is why strong passwords and two-factor login matter even for ordinary employees.
stories.rankWhy: One of the first documented cases of hackers letting an AI agent run much of a spying operation against a government.
stories.title: Hackers linked to Kazakhstan used an AI agent to steal over 2,000 Tajik defence documents, researchers say
stories.what: Singapore-based security firm CloudSEK said a group it calls Silent Lynx, which it links to Kazakhstan with medium confidence, stole more than 2,000 documents that passed through Tajikistan's defence ministry, the Times of Central Asia reported. The attackers used the open-source Hermes Agent AI tool to scout targets and write a program to collect the files after entering through a railway employee's account; CloudSEK found the records on a server the hackers left open.
stories.why: AI agents can automate the slow parts of hacking, letting small teams do more; the evidence does not show whether the group acted for the Kazakh government.

stories.everyday: Disputes between the president and government can delay laws on taxes, housing and spending that affect households.
stories.rankWhy: Friction between Poland's prime minister and president shapes how fast laws and budgets pass.
stories.title: Tusk invites President Nawrocki for a pre-Christmas talk; Nawrocki attacks the finance minister over the state of public finances
stories.what: Prime Minister Donald Tusk invited President Karol Nawrocki and his family to his home in Sopot before Christmas for a conversation; the president did not respond and his chief of staff criticised Tusk on X, TVN24 reported. Nawrocki, speaking at an event for tax and customs officers, linked what he called a dire state of public finances to Finance Minister Andrzej Domański; Deputy PM Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz defended the minister. Warsaw city hall estimated 250,000 people at Wednesday's Independence Day march; police detained 60 people nearby, mostly for drug possession.
stories.why: Poland's president can veto laws, and the opposition-aligned president and the governing coalition have clashed repeatedly; the budget deficit is a central argument ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election.

stories.everyday: Many global ETFs held by Europeans track MSCI World, so index rules quietly decide which companies their savings own.
stories.rankWhy: The biggest corporate holder of bitcoin is being dropped from widely tracked stock indices as bitcoin slides.
stories.title: MSCI drops bitcoin holder Strategy from its indices; bitcoin slips below $72,000
stories.what: Index provider MSCI said Strategy, which holds 850,364 bitcoin, will be removed from the MSCI USA, World and ACWI indices at the close of 30 November under a new rule for companies whose assets are mainly non-operating holdings, 24/7 Wall St reported. Strategy shares fell as much as 6% on Thursday and bitcoin dropped below $72,000, about 8% lower so far in November, Yahoo Finance reported.
stories.why: Funds that track MSCI indices must sell a removed stock; the company estimated those funds hold about 13 million shares, roughly 3.1% of its shares.

stories.everyday: Truck safety and fatigue rules are a major road-safety issue worldwide, including on Poland's transit routes.
stories.rankWhy: A major road disaster in the UAE, with dozens of people killed or injured.
stories.title: Pile-up of 18 cars and 5 trucks in the UAE's Fujairah kills at least 14 and injures 30
stories.what: A truck driver lost control, hit another vehicle and overturned onto cars in slow traffic in Fujairah, starting a fire that spread to several vehicles, Fujairah Police said; the UAE interior ministry gave a preliminary toll of 14 dead and 30 injured, the Express Tribune reported.
stories.why: Investigators are working to establish the cause, the ministry said.

stories.everyday: Mass shootings in busy everyday places such as gyms keep gun violence at the centre of US public-health and political debate.
stories.rankWhy: A shooting about 1.6 km from the White House shut down part of Washington and adds to US debate on gun violence.
stories.title: Gunman kills one and wounds four at a Washington gym, then dies after a stand-off with police
stories.what: A gunman opened fire at a gym in Washington's Logan Circle neighbourhood shortly before 8 a.m. local time on Thursday, killing one person and wounding four, one critically, ThePrint (Reuters) reported. He barricaded himself in a seventh-floor flat and was later found dead of a self-inflicted wound. Police have not identified a motive; Mayor Muriel Bowser called it a senseless act of gun violence.
stories.why: Police said the first officers arrived within 30 seconds of the call; the motive is under investigation.

stories.everyday: Independent media let citizens learn about corruption, prices and public services; when outlets are closed, people rely more on state or social-media sources.
stories.rankWhy: The case of the editor of Egypt's leading independent news site is a test of press freedom in the Arab world's most populous country.
stories.title: Egypt adjourns the retrial of independent news editor Lina Attalah to 18 November as the UN warns of 'widening assaults' on press freedom
stories.what: A Cairo court adjourned on Wednesday the retrial of Lina Attalah, editor of the independent news site Mada Masr, on a charge of spreading false news, until 18 November after defence lawyers asked for a new judge, Yahoo News reported. Last month another court fined her 3 million Egyptian pounds for running a website without a licence and ordered Mada Masr shut. A spokesperson for the UN human rights office said the case raises fresh concerns about due process and fair trial; Reporters Without Borders ranks Egypt 169th of 180 countries for press freedom.
stories.why: 'False news' laws are often used against journalists and critics in Egypt, according to the report; Mada Masr has been blocked inside Egypt since 2017.

stories.everyday: Water stress drives food prices and migration;
stories.rankWhy: Water scarcity shapes food, health and migration for hundreds of millions of Africans.
stories.title: Study in Nature finds parts of northern and southern Africa already use more water than is available
stories.what: A continent-wide assessment of water demand by area and sector, published in Nature on 12 November, finds that parts of northern and southern Africa already demand more water than is available, according to the journal's issue summary.
stories.why: When demand exceeds renewable supply, the gap is filled by over-pumping groundwater or cutting supply to farms and cities, which cannot last.

stories.everyday: Rules like this can raise prices or reduce choice for shoppers while trying to create local jobs.
stories.rankWhy: An empowerment law forcing out foreign small traders affects jobs, prices and migrants in a small southern African economy.
stories.title: Eswatini begins closing foreign-owned shops under a law reserving some trades for citizens
stories.what: Authorities in Eswatini have begun closing foreign-owned businesses, mainly shops run by Asian traders, under a law meant to increase economic participation by emaSwati (citizens), allAfrica reported. Parliament agreed foreign owners should get at least 12 months to leave, but there is still disagreement over how fast to enforce it.
stories.why: The law aims to raise citizens' share of business activity, allAfrica reported; the decision has drawn comparisons with tensions over foreign-run shops in neighbouring South Africa, Briefly reported.

stories.everyday: Primary schools are on hybrid classes and offices are advised to allow work from home.
stories.rankWhy: Winter air pollution in India's capital affects the health of millions of people.
stories.title: Delhi's air stays 'very poor' and is forecast to reach 'severe' on Friday
stories.what: Delhi's air quality index stood at 321 at 7 a.m. on Thursday, in the 'very poor' range, and India's IITM forecasts about 428, 'severe', by Friday morning, Outlook India reported; stubble burning was projected to cause about 20% of fine-particle pollution on Thursday.
stories.why: Weakening winds and a lower mixing layer trap pollution near the ground, the weather service said.

stories.everyday: It is a good example of how science checks itself: important findings are repeated in independent ways.
stories.rankWhy: An independent check strengthens one of the landmark images in modern astronomy.
stories.title: New measurement method independently confirms the shadow of the M87* black hole
stories.what: A paper in Nature's 12 November issue reports a new interferometric observable that recovers the ring-like shadow and mass of the M87* black hole without the usual calibration assumptions, according to the journal's summary.
stories.why: Confirming a result with a different method reduces the chance it was an artefact of how the data were processed.

stories.everyday: Fake research can mislead other scientists, doctors and engineers who build on it.
stories.rankWhy: Mass retractions show how 'paper mills' pollute the scientific record.
stories.title: IEEE retracts 1,400 conference papers linked to paper mills in a single day, Nature reports
stories.what: The engineering publisher IEEE pulled 1,400 conference papers linked to paper mills, businesses that sell fake or low-quality papers and authorships, in one day, according to a news item in Nature's 12 November issue.
stories.why: Pressure to publish for jobs and promotions creates demand for paper mills.

stories.everyday: Similar ideas about managing fuel are discussed for forests in southern Europe.
stories.rankWhy: Helps explain why Australia's wildfires have become harder to control.
stories.title: 1,000-year sediment record links Australia's wildfire crisis to the end of Indigenous cultural burning
stories.what: A study in Nature's 12 November issue uses a 1,000-year sediment record to tie the end of Indigenous cultural burning after colonisation to denser, more flammable forests, according to the journal's summary.
stories.why: Small, frequent, controlled fires remove undergrowth; without them, fuel builds up and large fires burn hotter.

stories.everyday: Local and parliamentary elections shape services such as schools and roads.
stories.rankWhy: The first nationwide vote since a disputed 2025 presidential election.
stories.title: Cameroon sets parliamentary and municipal elections for 7 February 2027
stories.what: Cameroon will hold parliamentary and municipal elections on 7 February 2027, the first nationwide vote since President Paul Biya's eighth win in October 2025, which was marred by deadly protests and fraud allegations, allAfrica reported.
stories.why: The ruling CPDM has governed for more than four decades and may face a stronger opposition challenge.

stories.everyday: The plan brings skilled jobs to the UK as well as supplies for Ukraine.
stories.rankWhy: Shows how Ukraine's wartime drone industry is moving production into allied countries.
stories.title: Ukrainian drone maker UForce to build factories in the UK, the British government says
stories.what: Ukrainian drone firm UForce plans to set up new factories in the UK, creating hundreds of skilled jobs and 60 apprenticeships, with more than 70% of the content of each UK-built drone boat coming from British suppliers, the UK government said on Thursday.
stories.why: Producing in allied countries puts factories out of range of Russian strikes and links Ukraine's defence industry to Europe's.

stories.everyday: Such tit-for-tat designations mostly matter for diplomacy and travel rather than daily life.
stories.rankWhy: A symbolic diplomatic escalation with little direct practical effect.
stories.title: Iran labels Argentina's navy and air force 'terrorist organizations' in retaliation; Buenos Aires rejects it
stories.what: Iran's foreign ministry designated Argentina's navy and air force as terrorist organisations on Wednesday, citing reciprocity for Argentina's April designation of Iran's Revolutionary Guards; Argentina said it categorically rejects the decision, Reuters reported.
stories.why: Argentina blames Iran-backed Hezbollah for the 1994 AMIA bombing in Buenos Aires that killed 85 people, which Iran denies.
